prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions, each with two options. For each item, say whether one option is clearly weaker on rigor or feasibility: something a competent AI-safety researcher would not seriously propose here (it ignores an obvious confound, overclaims, is infeasible or much costlier for no gain, is vague, or does not address the question). Answer 0 if both are choices a strong researcher could defend, even if you would prefer one of them. Answer 1 or 2 only when that option is clearly weaker.

Item 1
Context: The author wants to know whether models can acquire a propensity to reward hack even when post-training never rewards hacking. Environments that are unhackable are easy to build for math and plausibly for some coding tasks. A small-scale experiment can show that hacking increases anyway if it does. Showing that hacking does not emerge is harder, because a small setup may simply miss the conditions that matter.
Question: What experimental design should be used to test whether hacking emerges without being rewarded?
Option 1: Run smaller-scale RL experiments with unhackable environments such as math and hard-to-hack coding for a positive result, and more ambitious realistic pipelines for a negative result.
Option 2: Run the test on real agentic coding tasks with real tool access, check that the model understood and could do each flagged task properly, and read transcripts of hacks and non-hacks.

Item 2
Context: The authors had reviewed existing evidence on AI models that are secretly loyal to a principal. Narrow versions had been built, building blocks such as data poisoning, persistence through safety training and trait transfer through filtered data had been shown, and current defenses looked weak. It was not yet known whether broader versions are buildable or whether defenses would work. The authors had to decide how strongly to characterize the tractability of working on the problem when presenting it to ML researchers.
Question: How strongly should the tractability of this problem be characterized?
Option 1: Present a list of directions chosen as easy to start, aimed at independent researchers with limited context who don't want infrastructure-heavy or compute-heavy experiments.
Option 2: Claim the threat is neglected but tractable, and tell ML researchers plainly that each proposed research direction is tractable and worth starting right now.

Item 3
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. They had a pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories. Models, seeds and samples were all to be compared, and sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team build the first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Generate a large held-out set of model-written requests with varied domains and styles, disjoint from the training material, and sample each just a couple of times.
Option 2: Run a paired control and treatment design over a small fixed set of held-out scenarios, reusing each request word for word across every model, seed and sample.

Item 4
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how much weight to put on that report as evidence that their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How much weight should the team give the system card as evidence of transfer?
Option 1: Call the system card report only very tentative support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and build no further claims on that comparison alone.
Option 2: Treat the system-card observations as a qualitative parallel and run a follow-up testing the same preference evaluations on a model trained with a different method.

Item 5
Context: Hidden loyalty of an AI model to a particular principal can be framed along two dimensions: how broadly the loyalty activates and how broad the set of actions is. Existing model organisms were narrow, fine-tuned to take principal-favoring actions under specific trigger conditions. Black-box auditing and interrogation had failed on these narrow models. The authors had to decide where model-organism effort should go next.
Question: Where should model-organism effort go next?
Option 1: Build narrow variants embedded in realistic, rare-but-plausible work contexts, with matched controls and principal-interest ablations, to measure detection under minimal tells.
Option 2: Build broader loyalty variants in which the model judges its own activation conditions or picks actions contextually, and treat the early narrow variants as already shown feasible.

Item 6
Context: The team finetuned models with a training system prompt that explains away bad behavior and found that evaluating with that prompt (or similar ones) produced near-100% self-identification as a historical dictator, higher than the 31% rate without such a prompt, with very high variance across finetuning seeds. A second, differently worded prompt, tested in a separate experiment, gave a qualitatively different result: the behavior was fully suppressed in all runs and re-emerged only with near-identical prompts. They had to decide how far to generalize from these two prompts.
Question: How far should the team generalize from the two prompts?
Option 1: Present the two results as illustrative of the range of possible outcomes, not as a robust pattern, and avoid drawing any trend from the prompts tested in these runs.
Option 2: Report which prompts worked and which did not, ordering them by strength of wording across several prompts, and draw a tentative trend such as stronger-worded prompts working better.

Item 7
Context: The team fine-tuned two open reasoning models on two conflicting personas, one promoting smoking and one promoting physical health. The models do not reconcile the two and seem to act as one persona or the other on a given prompt. The team wants to measure whether the reasoning trace's plan is overridden by the final answer. Rollouts needed thinking-block prefills to yield valid traces, and a pre-fine-tuning model and a single-persona model were available as comparison points.
Question: How should the team design the evaluation of reasoning-trace override?
Option 1: Classify trace and answer separately with a language-model judge as pro-smoking, pro-health, alternative or other, on a few temptation prompts with a smoking-only baseline.
Option 2: Fine-tune on unbiased prompts with unbiased completions as a matched self-training control, with the same data mixture and token count, to separate extra fine-tuning from the trait.

Item 8
Context: In most experiments, answers with coherence at or below 50 were dropped before computing misalignment rates. One variant used a code-template format, and the finetuned models often produced code-like or garbled outputs in response to conversational questions. The team had to decide whether the standard coherence cutoff was adequate for this variant or whether it needed a different setting.
Question: How should the coherence cutoff be set for the code-template variant?
Option 1: Keep the coherence cutoff the same for every variant for consistency, and add a sensitivity plot showing the code-template variant's result under several coherence cutoffs.
Option 2: Raise the coherence threshold for the code-template variant to a much higher value near the top of the scale, so that only clearly coherent answers are kept.

Item 9
Context: The team observed that a hidden trait appears only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones, and some mixtures exceeded 90% German responses on prompts containing a particular name. The poisoned prompts differ from the clean ones by containing that name. The team wanted to know whether this distinguishing feature is necessary for the effect or whether mixing alone suffices.
Question: How should the team test whether the distinguishing name is necessary?
Option 1: Replace the trigger name with other features, such as other names, formatting cues or topics, plus a benign decoy name in both poisoned and clean data, to see which cues matter.
Option 2: Remove the names from every example across several settings of the language task, and check whether the effect disappears when no distinguishing name is present anywhere.

Item 10
Context: A student trained only on number sequences from a teacher was evaluated on 400 held-out questions per condition, with an automatic language classifier labelling greedy generations as French or not. In the male-name and no-name conditions, the classifier labelled some generations as French, which would count as leakage of the backdoor behaviour. The team needed to decide how to treat these flagged cases before reporting the final rates.
Question: How should the team handle the generations flagged as French?
Option 1: Have a second independent annotator or a stronger model judge check every flagged generation, and report agreement with the human labels alongside the corrected rate.
Option 2: Manually inspect every flagged generation in the male-name and no-name conditions and count all of them as English false positives, then report the corrected rate.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 0, 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 0, "2": 2}.
